rationales.A: Federal protection of Indigenous sovereignty was inconsistent and often absent.
rationales.B: The case sits in a long pattern: United States expansion repeatedly colliding with Indigenous sovereignty. From removal to allotment, expansion pressed against treaty rights again and again.
rationales.C: Presidential power in Indian affairs remained significant; it did not decline steadily.
rationales.D: Southern states actively pushed expansion; they did not refuse to take part.
rationales.general:
1. Name the collision. Expansion meets a distinct community occupying its own territory.
2. Ask whether it repeats. The same collision recurs across the nineteenth century.
3. Test the other continuities. Protection was inconsistent, presidential power stayed significant, and Southern states pushed expansion.
4. Match the pattern. Worcester shows expansion and sovereignty in conflict, again.
Remember: a continuity is a conflict that keeps returning in new forms.

stimulus.text: “The Cherokee Nation . . . are . . . a distinct community, occupying its own territory . . . in which the laws of Georgia can have no force . . . The Acts of Georgia are repugnant to the Constitution, laws, and treaties of the United States.”
